questions.question: What allows particles of a liquid to move through a material by diffusion?
options: If the material is magnetic
If the material is permeable
If the material is solid metal
If the material is completely waterproof

questions.question: In a practical investigation, what can be seen when a colored liquid diffuses into a plain jelly cube?
options: The liquid stays only on the outer surface of the cube without entering.
The jelly cube immediately melts into a liquid state.
The color slowly spreads inwards from the outer edges of the jelly cube.
The jelly cube turns into gas and disappears.

questions.question: What is the predicted effect of increasing temperature on the diffusion of a colored liquid into a jelly cube?
options: Diffusion happens at a faster rate.
Diffusion stops completely.
Diffusion slows down.
Temperature has no effect on the speed of diffusion.

questions.question: If you compare a small jelly cube and a large jelly cube, which one will have its center reached by a diffusing liquid first?
options: The larger cube because it has a larger surface area.
The smaller cube because the liquid has a shorter distance to travel to the center.
Both will reach the center at the exact same time because size does not affect diffusion.
Neither, because liquid cannot diffuse into jelly.

questions.question: Why do particles diffuse faster into a jelly cube at higher temperatures?
options: The particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.
The particles become heavier and sink quicker.
The jelly cube expands and creates massive visible holes.
The particles stop colliding with each other.

questions.question: Why can only certain substances pass through a selectively-permeable membrane?
options: Only magnetic particles can pass through.
Their particles are small enough to fit through the tiny holes in the membrane.
The membrane dissolves when touched by any substance.
Only particles that carry a negative charge can pass.

questions.question: When diffusion occurs across a selectively-permeable membrane, in which direction do the individual particles move?
options: Only from the left side to the right side of the membrane.
Only from the higher concentration side to the lower concentration side.
In both directions across the membrane.
They do not move through the membrane, only along its surface.

questions.question: If there is a high concentration of glucose inside a Visking tubing bag and a low concentration in the surrounding water, what is the net movement of glucose?
options: Net movement of glucose out of the bag into the water.
Net movement of glucose from the water into the bag.
No net movement because glucose cannot pass through.
Glucose will move in a circular motion inside the bag only.

questions.question: In an experiment using Visking tubing filled with starch and amylase, what is observed regarding the net movement of starch particles?
options: Starch easily diffuses out because its molecules are extremely small.
There is no net movement of starch out of the tubing because starch molecules are too large to pass through.
Starch moves out of the tubing rapidly by active transport.
The Visking tubing dissolves completely in the presence of starch.

questions.question: If iodine turns blue-black in the presence of starch, and iodine diffuses into Visking tubing containing starch, what is the correct explanation for the inside of the tubing turning blue-black?
options: Starch molecules diffused out of the tubing to meet the iodine.
Iodine molecules are small enough to diffuse through the tubing membrane into the starch solution.
The membrane of the tubing broke down completely.
Water molecules pushed the starch out of the tubing.

questions.question: Which statement is true about the composition of cell cytoplasm?
options: It is a continuous solid block with no individual components.
It is made up of particles, just like all other substances.
It contains only water and is completely free of any particles.
It is made of empty space with no matter in it.

questions.question: How do small substances like oxygen enter a living cell?
options: By passing through tiny holes in the cell membrane.
By breaking the cell membrane apart completely.
By dissolving the cell wall and entering through a vacuole.
By attaching to the outside of the cell without entering.

questions.question: Why are some substances, like large starch molecules, unable to diffuse into a cell?
options: They are repelled by the cell's electric field.
They are too big to pass through the holes in the cell membrane.
They are too heavy to move at all.
They are liquid, and only gases can enter cells.

questions.question: What makes a cell membrane 'selectively-permeable'?
options: It allows all substances to pass through freely.
It allows only certain substances to diffuse through it.
It blocks every single substance from entering the cell.
It can only let water pass through but nothing else.

questions.question: In which direction is the net movement of oxygen particles across a cell membrane when respiration is happening inside the cell?
options: Up a concentration gradient, from low concentration to high concentration.
Down a concentration gradient, from high concentration outside to low concentration inside.
There is no net movement because oxygen cannot pass through the membrane.
In a random direction that depends on the cell's shape.

questions.question: How do particles behave in a fluid during diffusion?
options: They move in perfectly straight parallel lines without touching.
They move in random directions and collide with each other all the time.
They stop moving completely once they are evenly spread.
They only move when an external force like gravity pulls them.

questions.question: What is meant by the 'concentration' of a substance in a liquid or gas?
options: The total weight of the container holding the substance.
The number of particles in a specific volume of the liquid or gas.
The temperature of the liquid or gas.
The speed at which the particles are moving.

questions.question: What does it mean when we say the net movement of particles is 'down a concentration gradient'?
options: Particles move from an area of lower concentration to an area of higher concentration.
Particles move from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
Particles move only downwards due to gravity.
Particles move in a circle around the highest concentration point.

questions.question: What is the definition of diffusion?
options: The active transport of particles using energy from respiration.
The passive movement of particles from an area of higher to lower concentration.
The movement of water through a semi-permeable membrane only.
The chemical reaction between two different gases.

questions.question: Why do particles spread out from an area of high concentration to low concentration during diffusion?
options: Because they are repelled by the container walls.
Because of their random motion and constant collisions.
Because they are actively swimming towards empty space.
Because they always follow magnetic fields.
